name: Dehydration cuts / water cutting
lead: Water cutting, or a dehydration cut, is the practice of temporarily reducing body water, through water and food manipulation, sweating, sweat suits or saunas, so that the body weighs less or looks drier and more defined. It comes from weight-class sports such as combat sports and rowing, where athletes lose water in the last days before a weigh-in to qualify for a lower class [1]. Physique competitors and people dressing for photos or events use the same idea for looks: the aim is to reduce the water held under the skin so that muscle outlines, veins and the jawline read more sharply.

In bodybuilding the practice is part of what is called peak week, the final days before a show, when competitors manipulate carbohydrate, sodium and water intake in pursuit of a look described as full and dry [2][3]. Reviews describe the stated goal as losing extracellular, subcutaneous water while holding on to water inside the muscle [2].

Sports regulators, emergency physicians and review authors have documented risks, including deaths of combat-sports athletes between 2015 and 2017 after extreme cuts [1]. Reviews of bodybuilding practice state that the effect of dehydration on physique appearance has not been studied and that serious case reports exist [2][3].

chain: Water intake, sodium, sweating or heat exposure are manipulated
Water held under the skin (subcutaneous fluid) is reduced temporarily
Muscle separation, veins and facial angles look sharper for a short window
angle.text: Practitioners cut water to look drier and more defined for a stage, shoot or event, targeting the fluid under the skin rather than fat. The effect described is short-lived and is reversed by rehydration [1][2].

paras: Weight cutting covers two different things: losing fat and muscle over the weeks before an event, and losing water in the last days before competition. The second form is what is popularly called water cutting [1]. Reported methods include restricting food, water loading, and sweating through exercise, a sweat suit or a sauna [1].
Weight is regained afterward by rehydrating and eating, which is why the change is temporary. Combat-sport athletes rehydrate between weigh-in and the bout [1].

Bodybuilders describe peak week manipulations of carbohydrate, sodium and water as a way to raise muscle glycogen, reduce subcutaneous water and limit bloating. A 2021 review by Escalante and colleagues in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation notes that competitors seek to lose extracellular water while preserving intramuscular water, citing earlier work indicating that as dehydration progresses, extracellular and intracellular losses approach a one-to-one ratio [2].

A 2014 review by Helms, Aragon and Fitschen in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition described competitors using fluid and electrolyte manipulation in the final days and hours before a contest [3]. A survey cited in a 2024 narrative review of carbohydrate loading reported that most natural bodybuilders used some form of peaking strategy the week before competition, mostly involving carbohydrate, water or sodium changes.

Researchers who have reviewed the topic state that the effect of dehydration and electrolyte manipulation on visual appearance has not been studied [3]. Both reviews note that over-dehydration could produce a flat, depleted look with less muscle fullness, because total body water and muscle water fall together [2][3]. Escalante and colleagues describe loss of the muscle pump and a withered look as outcomes of going too far [2].

In December 2015 a 21-year-old Chinese MMA fighter, Yang Jian Bing, died of dehydration while cutting weight for a ONE Championship bout. The promotion then banned dehydration-based cuts, moved to walking-weight arrangements and introduced urine specific gravity testing up to three hours before bouts. Muay Thai fighters Jordan Coe (March 2016) and Jessica Lindsay (November 2017) also died after cutting weight [1]. Emergency physician Paddy Golden described acute water loss as very dangerous and called for hydration testing [1].
In 2022 the Mohegan Tribe Department of Athletic Regulation suspended a fighter for six months and fined him $2,500 after he posted a video of himself vomiting during a cut [1].

For bodybuilding, Escalante and colleagues write that current evidence does not indicate that water and sodium manipulation is specifically effective or safe, and they cite case reports of hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, water intoxication, rhabdomyolysis and severe hypokalemia [2]. Nutrition experts rarely give advice on cutting weight and generally recommend against it, according to Wikipedia [1].

No controlled studies have tested dehydration cuts for cosmetic definition. Related research includes a 2019 survey of self-reported weight-cutting methods among professional mixed martial artists [1], a 2013 position statement prepared for the IOC Medical Commission on minimising health risks in weight-sensitive sports [1], and the two peak-week reviews above, which conclude that bodybuilder-specific data on water and sodium manipulation are lacking [2][3].

lore.intro: In physique communities the idea circulates mainly as a way to look drier for a shoot or show, and in combat-sport communities as a weigh-in routine. Community claims below reflect that general framing.

claims.claim: Dropping water makes you look more shredded for a day
claims.believers: Practitioners say that less subcutaneous water lets muscle definition and vascularity show for a stage appearance or photos [2].
claims.experts: Helms and colleagues state that the effect of dehydration and electrolyte manipulation on appearance has not been studied and that it may not improve appearance [3].

claims.claim: Water cuts are manageable if done briefly
claims.believers: Athletes who cut routinely describe it as a normal part of competing, with rehydration afterward [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia and the emergency physician it cites describe acute water loss as very dangerous, and combat-sports deaths followed extreme cuts [1]. The Escalante review cites case reports of electrolyte disorders in bodybuilders [2].

claims.claim: Cutting water while keeping glycogen high keeps the muscles full
claims.believers: Bodybuilders describe aiming to lose subcutaneous water while retaining intramuscular water, helped by carbohydrate loading [2].
claims.experts: The 2021 review says the evidence for these practices is sparse and that over-dehydration can cause flatness [2].

card.summary: Sweating and fluid manipulation to look drier; borrowed from combat sports, where extreme cuts have contributed to deaths.
card.aka: Water cut, dehydration cut, weight cutting
card.note: Deaths have been reported in athletes after extreme dehydration cuts.

quick.overview:
Water cutting means deliberately losing body water, via sweating or fluid manipulation, to weigh less or look leaner temporarily.

It comes from combat sports and rowing; looksmaxxing and physique circles borrow it for a drier look.
quick.mechanism: Fluid is removed from the body over hours to days, often with sauna or sweat-suit use and changes in water intake, then regained afterwards.
quick.risks: Combat-sports deaths in 2015 to 2017 followed extreme cuts, and regulators and physicians describe acute water loss as very dangerous. Nutrition experts generally advise against it.
